soap.subjective:
Basic information: 43 years old, female. Chief complaint: right knee pain following a fall from a ladder while changing a light bulb.

History of present illness: The patient fell off a ladder while changing a light bulb, resulting in injury to the right knee. The pain is located on the inside of the knee and has not been significantly relieved by ice or ibuprofen. The pain worsens with bending or twisting the knee. No swelling, bruising, instability, locking, clicking, or giving way of the knee has been reported. The patient can fully extend the knee, but it hurts when bending it. It is uncomfortable, but she can still move it a little. There is definitely pain when flexing it or twisting it. The patient has not been able to bear weight on the right knee much since the injury; it is pretty painful when trying, so she has been using crutches to keep pressure off of it.

Past history: No prior knee injuries or surgeries. Only nasal surgery. No history of arthritis or ligament tears in the knee.
soap.objective:
Physical examination: Physical examination findings: No swelling, bruising, instability, locking, clicking, or giving way of the knee. No numbness, tingling, or weakness in the right leg or foot. The patient can fully extend the knee but experiences pain when bending it or twisting it. Range of motion is limited due to pain. Ligament stability and meniscal injury assessment to be determined.

Investigations: Imaging studies: None reported.
soap.assessment:
Preliminary diagnosis:
Right knee contusion with possible meniscal involvement; Medial collateral ligament (MCL) strain; Patellofemoral pain syndrome

Diagnostic discussion:
The patient is a 43-year-old female who sustained a fall from a ladder, resulting in right knee pain localized to the medial aspect. The pain worsens with bending or twisting, and she has limited range of motion due to pain. She has not experienced swelling, bruising, instability, locking, or giving way, and she can fully extend the knee. The absence of swelling, bruising, or instability suggests a less severe injury, but the pain with flexion and twisting raises concern for a soft tissue injury, ligament strain, or early meniscal involvement. The lack of prior knee injuries or surgeries and absence of arthritis or ligament tears in the past history supports a traumatic etiology. The physical exam findings are consistent with a contusion or strain, but further imaging is needed to rule out meniscal or ligamentous injury. Differential diagnoses include right knee contusion with possible meniscal involvement, medial collateral ligament (MCL) strain, and patellofemoral pain syndrome.
soap.plan: 1. Further evaluation: Obtain an MRI of the right knee to assess for ligamentous or meniscal injuries. This is indicated due to the mechanism of injury and the presence of pain with twisting and bending. 2. Medication: Prescribe nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) such as ibuprofen for pain and inflammation, with caution for gastrointestinal or renal side effects. If NSAIDs are contraindicated, consider acetaminophen as an alternative. 3. Non-drug management and education: Advise the patient to avoid weight-bearing on the affected knee and continue using crutches. Recommend rest, ice, and elevation for pain relief. Encourage gentle range-of-motion exercises as tolerated. Educate on signs of worsening pain, swelling, or instability that would require urgent evaluation. 4. Follow-up: Schedule a follow-up in 1-2 weeks after the MRI results are available. If the MRI is normal and symptoms improve, reassess for return to normal activities. If there is no improvement or worsening symptoms, consider referral to orthopedics for further evaluation.
